column4: The section names root ʿ-s-r for the debtor's restricted means and dictionary form al-maysara for abundance. This ayah stages that debtor directly: give time until ease, or forgive the debt as charity.

The section's dictionary form dhikr al-ḥaqq means a debt note; this ayah orders a term debt recorded and says one witness may remind the other (tadhakkira, root dh-k-r). It makes the ledger image literal.

The section connects al-ʿusr and al-yusr with a change in means. This ayah orders spending according to one's means and promises ease after hardship (ʿusr, root ʿ-s-r; yusr, root y-s-r), in the same divine voice.

The section explicitly recalls the previous surah's wording: God found the Prophet poor (ʿāʾilan) and enriched him (aghna). That remembered change from want to sufficiency fills out its empty-to-full-hand image.

The section's wording waḍaʿnā ʿanka (root w-d-ʿ) is heard as a creditor laying down a claim; here the same root and ʿan construction say the messenger removes people's burden and fetters. The verse gives a direct image of release, though its burden is religious rather than financial.

The section turns 94:2 into a creditor's reduction of a debt. In this immediately surrounding debt ruling, a repentant lender keeps principal, with neither party wronging the other; that sets a precise limit on what may be claimed from a debtor.

The section hears the debt reduction as an act of charity. This ayah contrasts God erasing usury with increasing charities (ṣadaqāt), giving the image's waiving of a claim a clear opposite to extracting an increase.

The section pictures a debtor in straits and a creditor who can ease that strait. This ayah names debtors (al-ghārimīn) among the recipients of obligatory charity, joining debt relief to provision for people in need.

The section's cited expression measures voluntary charity by wealth left after dependents. Asked what to spend, this ayah answers al-ʿafw, the surplus, giving a direct Quranic counterpart to that measure.

The section describes short means as little in the hand and ends with the hand emptying or filling. This ayah pictures a hand bound to the neck or stretched out completely, then marks a measured course between withholding and exhausting one's means.

The section places 65:7's spending-by-means rule in divorce maintenance. This preceding ayah gives the concrete case: provide for pregnant divorced women until birth and pay them for nursing, so the following rule has an actual household obligation in view.

The section places the debtor's respite after the prohibition of usury. This adjacent command to abandon the remaining usury frames the later instruction to wait for an insolvent debtor as a boundary against continuing to extract more.

The section locates the debtor's relief just after the usury ruling. This ayah distinguishes permitted trade from forbidden usury, supplying the financial setting in which a lender may either claim an increase or ease the debtor's account.

The section connects remembrance to a written debt claim. Following the writing rule, this ayah handles a debt when no scribe is available through collateral and an entrusted borrower's duty to discharge the trust.

The section develops debt and then voluntary charity. This ayah calls spending for God's sake a good loan that is multiplied, using the same creditor-and-advance transaction image with God as the recipient.

The section's debt scene makes a financial claim tangible. This ayah calls giving to God a good loan and promises its multiplication; the lender is God-directed rather than a human creditor, a distinct but concrete use of the same transaction image.

The section links debt and charity. This ayah places men and women giving charity beside those who lend God a good loan, then promises multiplication, joining the two practices the section brings together.

The section hears a cancelled human claim as charity. This ayah describes giving as a good loan to God, to be multiplied and forgiven, a specific reversal in which the divine creditor repays the giver with increase and pardon.

The section stages a creditor and a borrower whose funds are entrusted or owed. This ayah contrasts a person who returns a large entrusted sum with one who will not return even a small coin unless pressed, making repayment and insistence on a claim concrete.

The section names roots ʿ-s-r and y-s-r while applying their hardship/ease pair to restricted and ample means. In the fasting rule, God intends ease (al-yusr) rather than hardship (al-ʿusr); the same pair is used for bodily religious difficulty, a distinct sense from debt.

The section pairs want and abundance through roots ʿ-s-r and y-s-r. In this surah's account of giving and withholding, God makes the generous, God-conscious person easy for the easy course (al-yusrā); here the ease is a moral path rather than wealth.

The section's debt scene turns on how a creditor treats an insolvent borrower. This prohibition of multiplied usury is a boundary against growing a claim through compounding it while the debtor is pressed.
The section's creditor can use a claim either to press the insolvent or to release him. This ayah condemns taking usury despite its prohibition, a concrete opposite to easing the debt.

The section brings a debt claim beside voluntary charity. This ayah contrasts wealth given as usury to grow people's property with zakat given seeking God, a direct monetary contrast between extraction and charitable giving.

The section interprets 94:2 through a creditor's claim and a charitable waiver. This covenant ayah also uses the concrete phrase “lend God a good loan” for giving wealth; the lender's recipient and promised return differ from the section's human debt.

The section links charity to its debt image. In a passage about prayer, alms and people's acts, this ayah also calls giving to God a good loan, a separate but explicit use of lending language for voluntary provision.

The section describes a person with means choosing whether to ease another's hardship. This ayah addresses people of bounty and abundance, tells them not to withhold from relatives and the needy, and calls them to pardon and overlook, meeting both abundance and forgiveness.

The section's creditor can turn a demand into release by forgiving the debt. This ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, giving a specific ethical boundary for aid that would otherwise harm or humiliate its recipient.

The section joins hardship, means, and charitable release. This ayah praises those who spend in both prosperity and adversity and pardon people, so it links giving across circumstances with the creditor's choice to forgive.

The section's charity citation measures giving from what remains after dependents. This ayah describes the servants' spending between extravagance and stinginess, making moderation a specific counterpart to that measure.

The section concerns restricted means and giving to a debtor in need. This ayah names poverty as the threat that can deter spending, then contrasts it with God's promise of forgiveness and bounty; it supplies the giver's side of the same pressure.

The section makes the weight lifted in 94:2 concrete through a written-off debt. This prayer asks not to have a burden laid on the community or what it cannot bear, and closes by asking pardon; its burden is moral, not financial.

The section's root ẓ-h-r names the back strained by a load. This verse pictures people carrying their burdens on their backs at judgment, a contrary bodily image that clarifies the section's movement from an imposed weight to release.

The section's dictionary gloss for al-ʿusr is restricted means and its counterword al-maysara is abundance. This ayah pictures a person receiving plentiful provision and mistaking it for honor, setting up the exact wealth contrast continued in the next ayah.

The section describes a person falling from plenty into straitened means. This next ayah says a person mistakes restricted provision for humiliation; the continuation in 89:17–20 turns to neglected orphans and feeding the poor, giving the economic contrast an ethical consequence.

The section names root ʿ-s-r for distress, especially lack of means. This ayah calls the Tabuk campaign the hour of hardship (sāʿat al-ʿusra), using the same hardship word for a collective, resource-strained trial rather than a private debt.

The section centers someone unable to pay because of straitened means. In the adjacent campaign passage, this ayah excuses the weak, sick and those who cannot find what to spend when they are sincere; it makes inability to provide a real limiting condition.

The section attends to the embarrassment of a person in material straits. This adjacent ayah describes people who cannot find mounts to go with the army turning away with tears because they have nothing to spend, a specific scene of inability rather than unwillingness.

The section's cited expression presents charity from wealth left after dependents. This ayah sets a more demanding measure: righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves, so the image opens from surplus toward costly generosity.

The section names a deduction from capital and pictures a debt account. This inheritance rule allocates shares only after a bequest or debt is discharged, treating the debt as an amount settled before the remaining property is divided.

The section's creditor-debtor image concerns a claim against available property. This inheritance rule likewise calculates family shares after a bequest or debt, showing how a debt reduces the estate before distribution.

The section presents a debt as a measurable claim on property. This final inheritance rule again places bequests and debts before the division, a concrete legal instance of settling the account first.

The section names al-yusr as abundance and dhikr as the remembrance associated with a debt note. This refrain says God made the Qur'an easy for remembrance (yassarnā ... li-l-dhikr), bringing both named roots together in different senses: ease of recitation and remembrance of revelation.

The section names roots y-s-r and dh-k-r for ease/abundance and remembrance. This repeated refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, a distinct meeting of the two roots from the section's economic and debt-note senses.

The section names roots y-s-r and dh-k-r for ease/abundance and remembrance. This repeated refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, a distinct meeting of the two roots from the section's economic and debt-note senses.

The section names roots y-s-r and dh-k-r for ease/abundance and remembrance. This repeated refrain says the Qur'an was made easy for remembrance, a distinct meeting of the two roots from the section's economic and debt-note senses.

The section explicitly separates the abundance sense of al-maysara from the ease sense of y-s-r. This promise that God will ease the Prophet toward the easier way uses the latter sense and the same divine voice as the surah's promise of ease.
The section names root ʿ-s-r for a debtor's hardship. Here ʿasīr names the difficult Day of Judgment, extending that root from material straits to an ultimate trial rather than a debt.
The section names al-yusr for ease alongside al-ʿusr for hardship. This next ayah says that day will not be easy for the deniers, completing the judgment-day reversal begun in 74:9.
The section uses al-ʿusr for restricted means, while this ayah calls the Day of Judgment ʿasīr, difficult for the deniers; the shared root carries difficulty beyond the financial sense.
The section names al-ʿusr for the strain of a debtor. This ayah calls the gathering day ʿasīr, a difficult day, using the same hardship word outside the financial setting.

The section's dictionary form al-maysara means abundance, while its root y-s-r also carries ease. In the same surah, the miser who treats himself as self-sufficient is eased toward hardship (al-ʿusrā), a reversal of the section's debtor receiving time and a creditor's possible generosity.

The section joins a strained back to a measurable financial load. This ayah requires full measure and just weight, then says God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity; together they set fair account and capacity beside the section's relieved burden.

The section's dictionary form waḍīʿa is a deduction from capital. In Shuʿayb's trade setting, this ayah forbids shortchanging people and requires full measure and weight, distinguishing a voluntary debt reduction from an unfair deduction in commerce.

The section's dictionary note also applies the root w-d-ʿ to commercial loss. Shuʿayb tells prosperous traders not to decrease measure or weight; the verse makes a commercial reduction an injustice rather than the generous write-off in the section.

The section's dictionary form waḍīʿa means an amount taken off capital. This continuation requires full measure and forbids depriving people of their goods, marking the contrast between an unfair shortfall and a creditor's voluntary reduction.

The section extends debt reduction into the image of an account being adjusted. This ayah requires full measure and just weight in trade, a boundary showing that lowering someone's debt is relief, while lowering their due goods is injustice.
The section cites waḍīʿa, a reduction from capital, as part of its financial image. Shuʿayb's command to give full measure begins a repeated warning against reducing what is owed to another.

The section's debt image depends on a measured amount being removed from an account. This next command requires weighing with a straight balance, completing the commercial measure whose deliberate reduction is condemned in this passage.

The section distinguishes a generous write-off from loss in commerce. This continuation forbids depriving people of their goods, giving the moral difference between reducing another's claim for their relief and shortchanging them.

The section's dictionary form waḍīʿa means a reduction from capital, and it mentions loss in trade. This ayah curses short-measurers, introducing the opposite case: reducing what is due to another is wrongdoing, not debt relief.

The section discusses trade loss and lowering an amount. This continuation says the short-measurer takes full measure for himself, showing the creditor's self-favoring side of an unjust account; 83:3 completes the under-measuring side.

The section's debt reduction is presented as a way to ease another's strait. This continuation says the short-measurer gives less when measuring for others, the contrary act of imposing a loss instead of forgiving one.

The section's cited expression measures charity from abundance left after dependents. This ayah praises people who prefer others even when they themselves have need (khaṣāṣa), a specific case beyond the surplus measure.

The section describes charity drawn from a person's means and a burden lifted from the back. This ayah warns that wealth people withhold will be made a collar around their necks, a reversal in which retained wealth becomes a burden.

The section links wealth to giving and to a load on the back. This ayah condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending it in God's way; the next ayah turns that stored wealth into a bodily burden.

The section's debt image makes release of a load concrete, and its charity citation names the back of wealth. This continuation brands hoarded gold and silver onto backs at judgment, the reverse image of wealth given to relieve need.

The section names root y-s-r for ease and cites 65:7's support rule. Earlier in the same divorce passage, this ayah promises ease in one's affairs to the God-fearing; 65:6–7 then gives the concrete maintenance and spending rules, so its ease promise belongs to that setting.

The section gives a secondary dictionary sense of loss in trade. This parable says the exchange of guidance for error did not profit its traders, using trade loss figuratively rather than for actual capital or debt.

The section imagines a creditor turning a claim into charity. This ayah's own contribution is the person who gives, is mindful of God, and affirms the good; 92:7 completes the image by describing ease for that course.

The section describes the creditor's choice to ease a debtor in straits. This ayah supplies the contrary disposition: a person withholds and deems himself self-sufficient; 92:10 completes that road with hardship.
The section connects generosity with relief of financial strain. This ayah urges spending and praises freedom from stinginess; 64:17 follows by expressing giving as a good loan to God.

The section explicitly likens its verses to a ledger and says a debt instrument may be called a remembrance. This ayah introduces each person's opened book at resurrection, a divine record rather than a creditor's note; 17:14 tells the person to read it and calls him his own reckoner.

The section's ledger image grows from the debt note it associates with remembrance. This ayah's own contribution is to make the person read his record and serve as his own reckoner; 17:13 supplies the opened book that it continues.

The section explicitly reads its first verses as an account ledger and connects remembrance to a written debt claim. This ayah presents a different ledger, a record that leaves no small or great deed uncounted; the link is the record-and-account image, not a human debt.

The section joins straitened means to a creditor's choice to relieve a vulnerable person. After the preceding ayah's contrast between ample and restricted provision, this ayah says people fail to honor the orphan; 89:18 continues with failure to urge feeding the poor.

The section's debt image asks the reader to see a person in need as someone who can be relieved. This ayah's own contribution is the failure to urge feeding the poor, continuing the social response to restricted provision begun in 89:17.
